Two shapes of front door

The properties sort into platforms and gateways. A platform puts the catalogue and the sign-up on the public side, and usually the documentation too. Visa, Mastercard, American Express, AP+ Developers, Dev.Elo and the UPI Open Platform work this way (Visa Developer Center, walked · Mastercard Developers, walked · American Express Developers, walked · AP+ Developers, walked · ELO, walked · UnionPay International Open Platform, walked). Visa still holds SDKs and sample code behind sign-in, American Express locks some API references, and AP+ gates its documentation pages (Visa Developer Quick Start · American Express, High-Level Process · Australian Payments Plus Developers). A gateway shows a welcome line and asks the reader to identify themselves before anything else: the Discover Developer Center, JCB Partner Online, EASI, the PULSE client website. The Interac Innovation Hub is a platform by shape and a gateway by rule, since access to specific products needs an existing relationship with an issuer (Innovation Hub, walked). Neither shape is wrong for a network that onboards through a sponsor and a contract. The difference is what a stranger can judge before asking to be let in.

What the account buys, and what the contract buys

Visa and Mastercard draw the same line for most products (Pricing on Visa Developer · Mastercard Developers, Quick Start Guide). The account buys a project, sandbox keys and mock data. The contract buys certification and production. Visa issues certification and production credentials only once a signed agreement is in place (Visa, Going Live), and says onboarding can take two weeks or several months (Visa Developer Onboarding). Mastercard mints production credentials instantly and leaves them inactive until it approves the production request (Mastercard Developers, Quick Start Guide), with a third environment, the Mastercard Test Facility, reached by emailing an implementation manager (Mastercard Developers, MTF Access Guide). American Express grants environment access, sandbox included, after a manual review of an access request, with the outcome sent by email (American Express Developers). It asks partners to accept legal terms before production only where they apply (American Express, Getting Started). Discover asks for the contact form first (Discover Developer Center, walked). At the other end, the Visa Acceptance and Authorize.net consoles come with default sandbox credentials (Visa Acceptance API Documentation · Authorize.net API Documentation). American Express says some public products open their sandbox without a request, yet its catalogue marks none of its eighteen products for instant access (American Express, High-Level Process).

Mock data, and who gets the test cards

No sandbox in this study replays production data. Visa's sandbox is mock data per project (Visa Developer Quick Start), Mastercard's returns generated account ranges that are not real BIN ranges (Mastercard Developers, BIN Lookup), and American Express describes its sandbox as mock data and static responses (American Express Developers). Test cards are public on the acquiring side and private on the network side: Visa Acceptance publishes test cards (Visa, Developer Center), Mastercard Send publishes test PANs that include other networks' (Mastercard Developers, Sandbox Test Cards), while Mastercard as a whole has no portal-wide test cards (Test Cards for Mastercard APIs) and American Express emails test cards after integration-setup forms (American Express Developers). Discover's test card kits sit inside EASI (Discover Network, walked).

Change and health

Only Mastercard publishes the health of every API for sandbox and production on a public page, refreshed about once a minute (Mastercard Developers, API Status). Visa Acceptance runs a Statuspage with subscriptions and an incident history, listing six sandbox areas beside its production services (Visa Acceptance Solutions Status). Visa Developer publishes monthly release notes tagged public or restricted (Visa, Release Notes). American Express's portal-wide changelog stopped in May 2024 while individual pages carry 2026 dates (American Express, What's New), and its urgent bulletins for network partners are posted inside the gated Knowledge Base (American Express, Insights). No public Discover site has a status page or a changelog, and EASI keeps its product announcements behind registration (Discover Partner Product Portal, walked · Discover Partner Product Portal · Discover Global Network, Tools to Enable Payments).

How many doors a partner meets

The number of places to sign in can be counted from the public pages. Visa has Visa Developer, Visa Partner, Visa Acceptance, the Visa Direct Partner Portal and the client website now branded Visa Access (Visa, Log · Visa Direct Partner Portal). Visa Access claims more than 150 services behind one password (Visa, Log). One Visa Partner account opens Visa Developer, Visa Partner and, after extra validation, Visa Access (Visa Partner Support and FAQ · Visa Developer Center, Frequently Asked Questions). Visa's technology partner site adds four sign-in portals, and Visa University has its own login (Visa, Home · Visa University). Mastercard has Developers and Connect. American Express has Developers, the Knowledge Base for network partners, the AMEX Enabled dashboard for service providers and the Online Merchant Account (American Express Global Network · AMEX Enabled Service Provider Program · American Express, Manage Payments Online). The Discover family has the Fraud and Risk Center, EASI, the Advanced Payments Providers portal, eCentral, the Disputes Portal, the Release Compliance Tool, Web Merchant Boarding, the Developer Center, a ServiceNow login for Diners Club issuers and the PULSE client website (Discover Network, walked · Discover Partner Product Portal, walked · Home, walked). The site's own Log In lands on the fraud tools and lists four of the others in a side panel. The Partner Product Portal also has a login page, though its login button is switched off, and it shares one sign-in service with the Disputes Portal (DFS Services, Discover Partner Product Portal).

Support routes

Support is where the networks differ most in tone. American Express takes a ticket from anyone, states its hours, and keeps product mailboxes (American Express Developers). Mastercard needs an account for a ticket and offers the forum, the guides and an MCP server to everyone else (Mastercard Developers, walked). PULSE publishes a phone number, Central-time hours and named mailboxes for disputes, fraud and the processor portal (Home, walked). Visa Developer offers FAQs and a contact form, and its community site did not answer on the day (Visa Developer Center, walked). Discover's Developer Center offers the contact form and nothing else (Discover Developer Center, walked).

The AI layer, in September 2026

Of the platforms walked, only Visa Developer runs an assistant of its own, and Mastercard and UnionPay publish MCP services for outside assistants to call (Visa Developer Center, Terms of Use · Mastercard Developers Agent Toolkit · UnionPay International Open Platform, walked). Visa Developer carries an Ask AI Assistant control in its header, its terms define an AI chatbot and an MCP code-generation service, and since 2026 it runs a documentation MCP server (Visa Developer Center, walked · Visa Developer Center, Terms of Use · GitHub, Documentation MCP Server). Visa also publishes a command-line package on npm described as AI-powered payments for Claude Code (npm registry, @visa/cli). Mastercard Developers ships an MCP server that works with Claude, Cursor and other clients, an agent toolkit page in its documentation, and llms.txt files in every footer (Mastercard Developers, walked). The UPI Open Platform led its hero with agentic payment solutions and MCP query services on the day (UnionPay International Open Platform, walked). American Express sells Agentic Commerce Experiences as a product but offers no assistant on the portal (American Express Developers, walked).

Behind the wall, on video

The partner portals that matter most are behind logins, and public video is the only way to see some of them work. The search ran a fixed query set per network across YouTube, the networks' own channels and conference and webinar archives, and kept 217 items out of more than 2,000 candidates, most of them cardholder material or advertising. Captions were read for 34 videos, 27 of them Mastercard's. YouTube stopped answering this study's caption requests partway through, so Visa, Diners Club and PULSE items are described from their public listings. A demonstration shows how a network presents a surface. It is not evidence of how the surface performs.

What video shows that the pages do not

Mastercard's tutorial puts a number on self-service: a four-field project form and sandbox credentials on the next screen (Mastercard News). The Gateway is the exception inside Mastercard. Its test merchant and its Click to Pay switch come from the merchant's bank or payment service provider, a route the developer site does not describe (Mastercard Merchant Cloud · scriptpapi). Payment facilitators are registered by their acquirer with a signed form on Mastercard Connect (Mastercard). American Express's Merchant website caps each payment search at 35 days from the previous 16 months (American Express UK). One Finicity recording puts API integration for lenders at about four weeks and calls contracting and onboarding the longest part (Mastercard Open Finance).

What no public video shows

No recording was found of Visa Access, Mastercard Connect's own screens, the American Express Knowledge Base or AMEX Enabled dashboard, any Discover partner tool, the STAR, NYCE or SHAZAM participant portals, JCB Partner Online, the AP+ member portal or UnionPay's institution portal. For those surfaces the public pages and their login walls are the whole of the public record.

What partners say

The sweep ran the same query set for every network across developer Q&A, code repositories, Hacker News, trade press, trade bodies and regulator submissions, from January 2023 to September 2026. It found 123 partner items: 19 favourable, 68 critical and 36 neutral or mixed. Two cautions shape the reading. Developer Q&A exists to report problems, so it leans critical by design, and trade-body statements are advocacy. Each quote below is one voice, never a verdict on a network.

The public record of partner opinion is thin. Of 231 network and audience cells, 1 reaches ten items from three sources, 11 hold three to nine, and 219 hold two or fewer. The only adequate cell is Mastercard's developers. Issuers, acquirers, ATM operators and program managers are almost silent in public for every network, which is itself the finding: the people who run these relationships do not discuss them where anyone can read.

Integration

Developer complaints cluster where the networks differ most from ordinary web APIs: request signing, mutual TLS, payload encryption and certificate handling. A recurring pattern is a call that works in the network’s own tester and fails from the developer’s code.

Who pays, and who owns the second network

Institutional voices argue about fees and about whether a second debit network is truly independent. Capital One’s ownership of PULSE and Discover is now part of that argument.

Australian Banking Association · RBA submission (Australian Banking Association) · September 2025 · trade bodies and regulators, favourable · (source)

“Flat-fee pricing for e-transfers, where financial institutions of all sizes pay the same rate, will help level the playing field.”

Competition Bureau Canada · Competition Bureau Canada news release · July 2025 · trade bodies and regulators, favourable · (source)

“It's made it very hard for new entrants to come up and scale.”

Daniel Eberhard, CEO, KOHO · The Logic · 2025 · fintechs, critical · (source)

What this could not establish

  1. What any network charges its partners by contract. Issuer rates, network assessments outside Canada, agent registration fees since 2016, production API prices and every US PIN network's switch fees are negotiated and unpublished (American Express 10-K 2025 · Pricing on Visa Developer · Mastercard Rules · Discover 10-K 2024 · PULSE Payments Network · Fiserv, STAR issuer brochure 01/23).
  2. The confidential rulebooks. The American Express network manual, Discover's operating regulations and U.S. acquirer fee chart, PULSE's and SHAZAM's rules and UnionPay's bylaws could not be read (American Express Global Network Policy · Discover Global Network, U.S. Acquirer Interchange Pricing · PULSE Network, Client Support · SHAZAM Payments Network · UnionPay International, Partner Institutions). Mastercard's rule announcements sit inside Mastercard Connect, behind its sign-in (Mastercard, Chargebacks Made Simple Guide · Mastercard Connect, walked).
  3. The inside of the partner portals. Every gated client portal in this study is described from its login page, its public documentation and public video only. That covers Visa Access, Mastercard Connect, the American Express Knowledge Base and AMEX Enabled dashboard and every Discover client portal. It also covers the PULSE client website, SHAZAM Access, JCB Partner Online, the AP+ member portal, UnionPay's institution portal and girocard's product-development site.
  4. Certification timelines. Visa puts going live on its developer platform at two weeks to multiple months, and Tap to Phone certification at six to twelve months (Visa Developer Onboarding · Visa, Tap to Phone). Mastercard's Mastercom and Send products publish durations, and Elo charges once custom certification passes 90 business days (Mastercard, Mastercom Onboarding Checklist · Mastercard Send Disbursements Onboarding Checklist · Regulamento dos Arranjos de Pagamento ELO, Versão). No other certification path in the study states how long it takes.
  5. API rate limits. No network publishes numeric limits. Mastercard's documentation uses placeholders, and Visa and American Express raise limits on request (Mastercard Developers, OAuth 1.0a and mTLS Error Codes · Visa Developer Error Codes · American Express Developers).
  6. Volumes and participant counts for the US PIN networks. STAR and Accel publish a combined figure only, and NYCE, SHAZAM, CULIANCE, Jeanie and AFFN publish none. The Federal Reserve's averages are the only comparable numbers (Accel and STAR Fiserv debit networks provide · Federal Reserve, Regulation II).
  7. Sites that refused this study. NPCI and RuPay blocked every fetch, so the RuPay profile rests on secondary sources. The live Cartes Bancaires site and Mastercard's marketing pages were read from archived copies (Wikipedia, RuPay · Browser Validation Page (Gcore)). The investor sites of Visa, Mastercard, Capital One and Fiserv returned bot walls, and filings were read on the SEC's site instead.
  8. Most demonstration captions. YouTube stopped answering caption requests partway through the study. Captions were read for 34 videos, and Visa, Diners Club and PULSE demonstrations are described from their listings. No video frames were captured.
  9. Most partner opinion. 219 of 231 network and audience cells hold two public items or fewer. Reddit, LinkedIn and several vendor forums could not be read without an account.
  10. Trade-press corroboration for the later networks. The research agents for the Discover family and the smaller networks ran out of search quota, so their profiles lean on primary documents and carry fewer Reported sources.
  11. 10 claims that failed re-verification. They were dropped from the report and remain in the ledger with the reason. Among them are Mastercard's Canadian and Australian interchange schedules of 2026, which no method could re-read, and a Canadian cross-border assessment whose only readable archive shows a different rate.
  12. What the walk counts measure. Clicks to documentation and clicks to the first wall come from a scripted walk that follows the first matching link. They are comparable between properties and are not a usability measure.

Method

Desk research, walkthroughs and sentiment gathering ran on September 25, 2026, against public sources only. Nothing behind a login was used for any network, including Discover, so the comparison is symmetric. No account was created, no credentials were entered and no form was submitted on any site. Cookie banners were declined where a decline existed and left unanswered where they were accept-only.

Every network was read against the same twelve dimensions: identity and reach, services by partner type, partner-facing surfaces, how a partner joins and certifies, documentation and sandbox, public pricing, operating rules, service and support, news since September 2024, sentiment by audience, the observed walk and recorded demonstrations. Each claim is a row in a ledger before it is a sentence, with the page it was read on, a verbatim quote of twenty-five words or fewer, the publisher, the date published where the page states one, the date read, and a label. Verified means read on a primary document: the network's own documentation, rules, fee schedules or filings, a regulator, a court, or the browser on the day. Reported means trade press, analyst work, practitioner writing, a forum post or a third-party demonstration. Vendor means the network's or a vendor's claim about itself with no outside check.

Walkthroughs ran logged out in a headless browser at 1440 by 1000 pixels through a fixed station script (landing, what is visible without an account, catalogue, documentation depth, the sandbox or sign-up path to its first wall, certification, support, status and change, search, an assistive check, the landing at 390 pixels, and the first useful artefact a stranger can obtain), and every property with a public partner surface was then read by hand in the browser pane. The rungs used to compare portals describe choices, not scores, and only two counts are reported as facts: clicks to documentation and clicks to the first wall.

Sentiment was gathered with one fixed query set per network (developer, API, sandbox, certification, onboarding, support, fees for acquirers, processors, merchants and ATM operators, plus two network-specific terms) over January 2023 to September 2026. Where a query returned thirty items or fewer, all were read. Otherwise the fifteen most relevant and the fifteen most recent were read and the report says so. Each item was coded by audience, stance and topic, and each audience is reported with its tier: Adequate at ten or more items from three or more sources, Thin at three to nine, Absent at two or fewer. Recorded demonstrations were found by the same query discipline across official channels, conference and webinar archives, podcasts and app stores. Only captions were pulled from video, never the file, and frames were captured from the public player at the timestamp cited.

Every figure, ownership statement, date, fee and absence claim was then given to three independent readers who were asked to refute it from public sources without seeing the original citation. A claim survives if two of the three could not refute it. Claims that failed, or whose page had changed with no archived copy, are listed in the section on what this research could not establish and are not carried as findings.

Source register

Every source cited in this report, by network, with the date it was read and its confidence label. Browser walks are listed with their station records.
